bible_refs.note: When you spread forth your hands, I will hide my eyes from you; yea, when you make many prayers, I will not hear.
Those who honor me I will honor, and those who despise me shall be lightly esteemed.

You have sown much, and brought in little; you have eaten, but not to satiety; you have drunk, but not to drunkenness; you have clothed yourselves, but no one is warm; and he who earns wages earns wages to put them into a bag with holes.
You looked for much, and behold, it came to little; and when you brought it home, I blew it away.
Ἀλλὰ διωξόνται ἔθνος ἔθνος ἐν ξίφει, καὶ οὐ μὴ δυσ gespielt... (the quoted phrase matches the LXX: 'they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks')
Χριστὸς χθὲς καὶ σήμερον, ὁ αὐτὸς καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας.
ὁ ἐκ Θεοῦ καὶ Πατρὸς ἀπαστράψαντι Λόγῳ alludes to the Word who was with God and became flesh.

choices.why: The verb καταρδεσθαι in this context conveys a petition or request directed toward God for seasonal provisions, fitting the agricultural metaphor; alternatives like 'seek' or 'desire' lack the supplicatory force.

In early Christian Greek, νάμαι (from νόμος) often denotes divine allotments or gracious provisions, especially in pastoral contexts; translating as 'produce' or 'crops' would miss the theological nuance of God-bestowed sustenance.

Pleonexia is a technical moral term in patristic Greek for avarice or covetousness, especially when tied to unjust gain; 'avarice' is close but less common in English theological discourse, while 'covetousness' is too narrow.

The compound verb ἐξουδενῶν carries a strong contemptuous sense of rendering someone or something worthless or negligible; 'despises' is close but weaker, while 'ignores' misses the active devaluation.
The noun denotes a settled attitude of despising, stronger than mere neglect; context shows it as the root of transgression.
The plural noun refers to specific acts of moral failure, not abstract sin; matches the enumeration of failures in later verses.
The compound verb implies active impiety; 'deeds' conveys the plural dative instrumental sense of mutual reinforcement.
The perfect indicative of ἐκβαίνω emphasizes the completed emergence of the prophetic word into present experience.

The phrase appears corrupted; 'θάτερος' is clear as 'the other', but 'θα τέρου' is likely OCR noise for a comparative like 'τὰ χείρονα' (the worse things), so I render it contextually as 'the worse things' to preserve meaning without inventing text.
The verb is aorist middle/passive of ἐφθέγγομαι, meaning 'to utter' or 'to speak', fitting the context of the harvest being declared ready.
The source has 'ζωννυμένῳ', a present middle participle of ζωννύμω, meaning 'girding oneself', here describing the plowman preparing for work; rendered as 'being girded' for English idiomatic flow.
The text shows a split 'ἀλγύ νεται' due to line break; this is clearly 'ἀλγύνεται' (present passive of ἀλγέω), meaning 'causes him pain', referring to the things over which one conquers.
The adjective modifies the implied noun 'wickedness' in predicate position, conveying its painful, piercing quality as experienced in the heart.

choices.english: it has reached to your heart
choices.why: The verb ἁπτομαι with ἕως indicates extension to a limit; the heart is the innermost part, so 'reached to your heart' conveys deep penetration.

choices.english: one ought justly to be punished
choices.why: The infinitive construction with χρῆναι expresses necessity; δικαίως modifies the passive verb, so 'justly to be punished' captures the moral obligation.
rejected: it is necessary to be justly punished

choices.term: ταῖς παρ' ἡμῖν ἀπο νοίαις ἰσοστατεῖν ἀνάγκη τὴν δίκην
choices.english: it is necessary to weigh against our opinions the judgment
choices.why: The phrase ἀπο νοίαις is a rare or corrupted form of ἀπὸ τῶν νοημάτων (from our thoughts/opinions); ἰσοστατεῖν means to balance or weigh against; the structure demands 'weigh against our opinions the judgment'.
rejected: it is necessary to balance the judgment with our thoughts
we must weigh our opinions against the judgment

choices.term: Συγκόψωμεν, καθὼς γέγραπται, τὰς ῥομφαίας εἰς ἄροτρα, καὶ τὰς ζιβύνας εἰς δρέπανα
choices.english: let us beat our swords into plowshares and our spears into pruning hooks, as it is written
choices.why: The cohortative ἐπίστημι (implied by Συγκόψωμεν) expresses collective action; the allusion to Isaiah 2:4 is explicit via καθὼς γέγραπται; the parallelism is preserved.
rejected: let us convert our swords into plowshares
we should beat our swords into plowshares

choices.english: we have sinned, we have been lawless, we have done wrong
choices.why: The triple perfect active indicative emphasizes completed action; the terms are distinct in nuance: ἁμαρτάνω (miss the mark), ἀνομέω (live without law), ἀδικέω (do injustice); the rendering preserves the cumulative confession.
rejected: we have sinned, transgressed, and done evil
we have missed the mark, lived lawlessly, and acted unjustly

choices.term: τότε γὰρ, τότε καὶ ἵλεως ἔσται Θεός
choices.english: for then, then God will be merciful
choices.why: The repetition of τότε emphasizes temporal sequence; ἵλεως is the merciful state of God; the future indicative ἔσται confirms expectation.
rejected: at that time God will show mercy

choices.term: ἀποστήσει μὲν τὴν ὀργὴν, εὑρήσει δὲ πάλιν ἡ γῆ
choices.english: he will turn away his wrath, and the earth will again find
choices.why: The future indicative ἀποστήσει and εὑρήσει are parallel; πάλιν with εὑρήσει implies restoration; the earth is the subject finding (what is implied from context: favor, fruit).
rejected: he will remove his anger, and the earth will find again
he will turn back his wrath, and the earth will rediscover

choices.why: The verb εὐφραίνω in middle voice here takes an indirect object; the sense is 'to cause joy' or 'to refresh' in context of divine gifts; 'refresh us' fits the agricultural and pastoral tone.

choices.term: μὴ δυνάμενον συμπαθῆσαι ταῖς ἀνομίαις ἡμῶν
choices.english: unable to sympathize with our lawlessness
choices.why: The negative participle modifies ἀρχιερέα; συμβαθῆσαι is the aorist infinitive of συμπαθέω; the dative ἀνομίαις indicates the object of sympathy.
rejected: not able to feel compassion for our sins
incapable of sharing in our lawlessness

choices.term: πεπειρασμένον δὲ καθ' ὁμοιότητα χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας
choices.english: but one who has been tested in likeness apart from sin
choices.why: The perfect passive participle πεπειρασμένος agrees with an implied subject (the high priest); καθ' ὁμοιότητα means 'in likeness'; χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας is 'without sin'.
rejected: tested like us but without sin
made like us in every way except sin

choices.term: πεχείρως ἐποι κτείρειν ἐθέλειν τῷ Μονογενεῖ
choices.english: for because it is at hand to do, I think I will need no effort to persuade anyone to be able
choices.why: The phrase is grammatically disrupted (likely OCR corruption of ἐγγὺς χείρως ἔστι ποιῆσαι τὸ ἐθελεῖν τῷ Μονογενεῖ); the sense is that acting in accordance with the Only-Begotten is readily possible; the rendering captures the author’s confidence in ease of compliance.
rejected: for it is easy to do what the Only-Begotten wishes
since it is near at hand to do what the Only-Begotten wills

choices.english: you suppose to agree with us
choices.why: The double verb is likely a corruption of συγκατατιθέμενοι ὑπολαμβάνετε (you suppose you are agreeing); the sense is that the audience is assumed to concur.
rejected: you agree to go along with us
you are thought to concur with us

choices.why: The verb δράω in this context means 'to act' or 'to do' in the sense of exercising power; the infinitive follows δύνασθαι naturally.
Standard theological phrase indicating inherent, essential status as opposed to acquired or relational attributes.
Literal rendering of the Greek idiom meaning 'forever' or 'eternally'; preserves the eschatological tone.

Thinking, and asking of God the yearly gifts for the field, upon nothing indeed of the good things concerning the riverbank reeds cutting, nor upon hunting the water-wandering creatures the boat; but having greed more for the tillage, defiling with unjust bloods the God-given gift, and granting favor to watery beasts akin to man; then what hands, tell me, do you stretch out to God? And what altogether do you say praying, or how do you ask for good things, God saying through one of the prophets: 'When you stretch forth your hands toward me, I will turn away my eyes from you, and if you multiply your prayer, I will not hear you;' for your hands are full of blood;' but the one who makes none of his laws of account, what further concern will be shown? 'Those who glorify me I will glorify, says the Savior, and the one who treats me as nothing shall be treated as nothing.' Therefore suppose to him the 77.564 goose, and repay the price, and bestow abundant provision upon all necessities, or unable to endure the yoke, and endure being punished; for if it is necessary to speak further on these things, to drink amid good things and to be filled with votive offerings, at times this very abundance for you has become the precursor of impiety; for such a thing also says the Lord of all gods: 'And they were filled to satiety, and their hearts were lifted up; on account of this I forgot them.' And truly dreadful indeed is the pleasure toward slipperiness; sufficient indeed to bring forth the progenitor of insensibility.

But bitter is the offspring of disobedience the contempt of God; but of the contempt in this the fruit, every kind of transgressions. Therefore when we see you suffering this, we will lament fittingly, and we will utter a prophetic voice, to your ungodly deeds mutually strengthening ourselves. 'Alas, soul, because the pious one who is from the earth and the one who accomplishes in humans does not exist. All are justified in blood; each one drags down his neighbor, they lift up their hands to evil upon the bad.' Upon these our transgressions justifiably we are indignant, and we are distressed, as is seen, God. 'Behold, behold the thing spoken through the prophets, unto us not once, but already many times, it has come forth.' 'Thus says the Lord Almighty: You have sowed much, and you have brought in little. You have eaten, and not to satiety. You have drunk, and not to drunkenness. You have clothed yourselves, and you have not been warmed by them. And the one who gathers wages, he has gathered into a bag with holes.' But also besides these he says: 'You have looked for much, and they have become little. And it has been brought into the house, and I have blown them away,' says the Lord Almighty. Let us see if these things have truly happened. Let someone show the one who rejoices passing by, and I have conquered, let him seek the tearless eye, and even if he finds it, I have ceased.

You are striving for the present, you Egyptian farmers dwelling on the land, upon only suffering the other the worse things, and the one conquering among you of those seeming to be defeated is weaker, for he conquers in the things which cause him pain, and he has a more prosperous misfortune from the labors of his neighbor, but the things which it was customary for you to boast about, after long times are absent, or perhaps not all calamities of us are filled with lamentations and tears, what then, tell me, do we see villages lying in some places? their earth indeed the blows coming from hail carrying, by famine and lamentation are wasted, nowhere entirely, even if perhaps to be grieved in moderation, helping, but the stalk already grown and tall, let someone reap it only now and it was uttered, and the one who had plowed the earth, having taken the unreserved helper, was delighted being girded for work, perhaps also not satisfying him the threshing floor often he considered, but these things were a dream, the work of shadow and hail, not of reaping, but the one who seemed already to be enjoying the good things, immediately all was empty, instead of the stalks wealth of hail, much and great of the hope he failed, but the village neighboring this and bordering having become accustomed milder anger, the ones upon the plows she mourns labors, but having cultivated long and broad field an easy thing, she counts wealth toward the present the food for satiety, but rather the much and exceedingly giving satiety, δ׳.

Your ways and your practices have brought these things upon you; this is your wickedness, because it is bitter, because it has reached to your heart; for it follows from transgressions that one ought justly to be punished, and it is necessary to weigh against our opinions the judgment; therefore let us cease from every impious daring; let us beat our swords into plowshares and our spears into pruning hooks, as it is written; and as the Melodist says, 'Come, let us worship and bow down before him,' and let us weeping say, 'We have sinned, we have been lawless, we have done wrong'; for then, then God will be merciful; and he will turn away his wrath, and the earth will again find, and with gifts according to custom will refresh us; for we do not have a high priest unable to sympathize with our lawlessness, according to the voice of Paul; but one who has been tested in likeness apart from sin; for because it is at hand to do, I think I will need no effort to persuade anyone to be able; but also you suppose to agree with us, gathering around the measure of love toward us, and understanding the magnitude of what he endured on our account.

Since indeed we all who inhabit this surrounding region were like fish caught in a net by the insatiable greed of the ruling demon, the Only-begotten became human so that he might deliver all, proclaiming release to captives and sight to the blind, as he himself somewhere says, and calling this the acceptable year of the Lord. Therefore the Only-begotten is merciful, even if the Jews, not understanding the manner of the dispensation, kept themselves from even wishing to take him, sometimes insulting and calling a Samaritan, sometimes again acting shamelessly grieved, and rushing into foreign madness, and daring already to lie down. But since he was convicting those fighting against God, and inquiring from them the cause of their unjudged madness, the Lord said: Many good works I have shown you from my Father. For which of these works do you stone me? They answered: Not about a good work do we stone you, but about blasphemy, because you, being a man, make yourself God. Then, what to them the Savior? If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me; but if I do, even if you do not believe in me, believe my works. For not from those things by which as a man he appeared to those seeing was he deemed worthy to be tested concerning himself, but from those things by which God worked, not having acquired the claim of divinity, as we do, when the divine Scripture says gods; but essentially existing more with him, both truly according to nature God, and by the hereditary law of the begetter's peculiarity.

And he also has the ability to do all things, not having received from another, but as Lord of the powers, and from the substance of God and Father. For if indeed he became man through the love toward us, but we should not by this be ignorant of the Lord of all things, nor should we cast out the Emmanuel who is by nature God, nor should we to the Jews who think the same things bring against him the charge of humanity on our account, nor should we say, impiously accusing the one who came to be on our account because of us apart from sin; we would not worship you, since, being a man, you make yourself God. For he was and is and will be God by nature, before flesh and after flesh. And Paul will also bear witness, writing: 'Christ yesterday and today, the same and into the ages.' Do you see how he is found not cutting the Emmanuel into a duality of sons, nor as happening to be naked by himself, the one who flashed forth from God and Father as the Word, to him he assigns having the same thing always; but one Son only and alone by nature.
pass_b_english: One who thinks to ask God for the yearly gifts of the field, yet cuts no riverbank reeds and hunts no water-wandering creatures in the boat, but instead clings greedily to the tillage, defiling the God-given gift with unjust blood and granting favor to watery beasts as if they were kin to man—what hands, tell me, do you stretch out to God? And what do you say in prayer, or how do you ask for good things, when God has declared through one of the prophets: 'When you stretch forth your hands toward me, I will turn away my eyes from you, and if you multiply your prayer, I will not hear you'—for your hands are full of blood?

Yet the one who disregards any of his laws, what further concern could possibly be shown toward such a one? For the Savior says: 'Those who glorify me I will glorify, and the one who treats me as nothing shall be treated as nothing.' Therefore, suppose to him the 77.564 goose, repay its price, and bestow abundant provision upon all necessities—or, if unable to endure the yoke, endure being punished. For if it is necessary to speak further on these matters, to drink amid good things and to be filled with votive offerings, at times this very abundance for you has become the precursor of impiety. For such a thing also says the Lord of all gods: 'And they were filled to satiety, and their hearts were lifted up; on account of this I forgot them.' And truly dreadful indeed is the pleasure toward slipperiness; sufficient indeed to bring forth the progenitor of insensibility.

But bitter is the offspring of disobedience—the contempt of God. And from this contempt in our midst springs every kind of transgression. Therefore when we see you suffering this, we rightly lament and raise a prophetic voice, strengthening one another against your ungodly deeds.

'Alas, soul,' we cry, 'because the pious one who is from the earth and the one who accomplishes good among humans does not exist. All are justified in blood; each one drags down his neighbor, lifting up their hands to evil.' Upon these our transgressions we are justifiably indignant, and we are distressed, as is seen, God.

'Behold, behold the thing spoken through the prophets,' we say, 'it has come forth to us not once, but already many times.' Thus says the Lord Almighty: 'You have sowed much, and brought in little. You have eaten, and not to satiety. You have drunk, and not to drunkenness. You have clothed yourselves, and you have not been warmed by them. And the one who gathers wages has gathered them into a bag with holes.'

But besides these he says: 'You have looked for much, and they have become little. And it has been brought into the house, and I have blown them away,' says the Lord Almighty. Let us see if these things have truly happened. Let someone show the one who rejoices passing by, and I have conquered, let him seek the tearless eye, and even if he finds it, I have ceased.

You Egyptian farmers, dwelling on the land, are striving for the present, yet you only suffer the worse things from one another, and even the one who seems to conquer among you is actually the weaker, for he conquers only in what causes him pain, and his victory brings him a more prosperous misfortune from his neighbor's labors. The things you once were accustomed to boast about have long since vanished. Or perhaps not all our calamities are filled with lamentations and tears? Tell me, do we see villages lying in some places? Their earth bears the blows of hail, and through famine and lamentation they are wasted—not entirely destroyed, to be sure, and even if one were to grieve only moderately, it would still help. But the stalk is already grown and tall; let someone reap it now, and it was uttered. The one who had plowed the earth, having taken the unreserved helper, delighted in being girded for work, though perhaps even this would not satisfy him, and he often considered whether the threshing floor would be enough. But these things were merely a dream—the work of shadow and hail, not of real reaping. Yet the one who seemed already to be enjoying the good things found immediately that all was empty. Instead of stalks, wealth came as hail—much and great—and thus his hope failed. But the village neighboring this one, and bordering it, having grown accustomed to a milder anger, mourns the labors of those upon the plows, yet having cultivated a long and broad field with ease, she counts her wealth toward the present as food for satiety, but rather as the much and exceedingly giving satiety.

Your ways and your practices have brought these things upon you. This is your wickedness, because it is bitter, because it has reached to your heart. For it follows from transgressions that one ought justly to be punished, and it is necessary to weigh against our opinions the judgment.

Therefore let us cease from every impious daring. Let us beat our swords into plowshares and our spears into pruning hooks, as it is written. And as the Melodist says, 'Come, let us worship and bow down before him,' and let us weeping say, 'We have sinned, we have been lawless, we have done wrong.' For then, then God will be merciful.

And he will turn away his wrath, and the earth will again find, and with gifts according to custom will refresh us. For we do not have a high priest unable to sympathize with our lawlessness, according to the voice of Paul. But one who has been tested in likeness apart from sin.

For because it is at hand to do, I think I will need no effort to persuade anyone to be able. But also you suppose to agree with us, gathering around the measure of love toward us, and understanding the magnitude of what he endured on our account.

We who dwell in this surrounding region were all like fish caught in a net by the insatiable greed of the ruling demon. Then the Only-begotten became human, so that he might deliver us all, proclaiming release to captives and sight to the blind, just as he himself somewhere declares, and announcing this as the acceptable year of the Lord. Therefore the Only-begotten is merciful, even though the Jews, not understanding the manner of his dispensation, kept themselves from even wishing to accept him—sometimes insulting him and calling him a Samaritan, sometimes acting with shameless grief, rushing into foreign madness, and daring already to lie down.

If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me; but if I do, even if you do not believe in me, believe my works. For not from those things by which as a man he appeared to those seeing was he deemed worthy to be tested concerning himself, but from those things by which God worked, not having acquired the claim of divinity, as we do, when the divine Scripture says gods; but essentially existing more with him, both truly according to nature God, and by the hereditary law of the begetter's peculiarity.
He possesses the power to do all things, not derived from another but as Lord of the powers, drawing his ability from the very substance of God and Father.

Although he became man out of love for us, we must not therefore ignore that he remains Lord of all, nor reject the Emmanuel who is God by nature, nor accuse those Jews who share our views of falsely charging him with humanity on our account.
We would not speak impiously against the one who came to be on our account, as if he were sinless because of us; nor would we worship you, since, being merely a man, you make yourself God.
For he was, and is, and will be God by nature, existing both before flesh and after flesh.

Paul will also bear witness when he writes: 'Christ yesterday and today, the same and into the ages.' You can see that he does not divide Emmanuel into two sons, nor treat him as if he were merely a naked man appearing by chance; rather, the Word who flashed forth from God and Father is granted the same divine status always.
But there is only one Son, by nature alone.

   συνάγων, συνήγαγεν εἰς δεσμὸν τετρυπημένον." Ἀλλὰ καὶ πρὸς τούτοις ἔτι
   φησίν· "Ἐπεβλέψατε εἰς πολλὰ, καὶ ἐγένοντο ὀλίγα. Καὶ εἰσηνέχθη εἰς τὸν
   οἶκον, καὶ ἐξεφύσησα αὐτὰ, λέγει Κύριος παντοκράτωρ." Ἴδωμεν γὰρ εἰ μὴ
   ταῦτα συμβέβηκεν ἀληθῶς. Ἐπιδεικνύτω τις τὸν χαίροντα παρελθὼν, καὶ
   νενίκημαι, ὀφθαλμὸν ζητείτω τὸν ἀδάκρυτον, κἂν εὕρῃ, πεπαύ σομαι.
   Φιλονεικεῖτε πρὸς τὸ παρὸν, οἱ τῶν Αἰγυπτίων οἰκοῦντες γηπόνοι, ἐπὶ μόνῳ
   τῷ παθεῖν θάτερος θα τέρου τὰ χαλεπώτερα, καὶ ὁ νικῶν ἐν ὑμῖν τῶν ἡττᾶ
   σθαι δοκούντων ἀθλιώτερος. Νικᾷ γὰρ ἐφ' οἷς ἀλγύ νεται, καὶ τῶν τοῦ
   γείτονος πόνων πλουσιωτέραν ἔχει τὴν συμφοράν. Τὰ δὲ οἷς ἦν ἔθος ὑμῖν
   ἐπαυχεῖν, μακροῖς ἤδη χρόνοις ἀποδημεῖ. Ἢ γὰρ οὐχὶ ταλαι πωρίας ἡμῖν
   ἁπάσης ἀνάμεστα καὶ δακρύων τὰ διηγήματα; Τί δὲ, εἰπέ μοι, τὰς κώμας ἔν
   τισιν ὁρῶμεν κειμένας; Ἡ μὲν γῆ αὐτῶν τὰς ἀπὸ χα λάζης ἐνεγκοῦσα πληγὰς,
   λιμῷ καὶ θρήνῳ μαραίνε ται, οὐδαμόθεν παντελῶς, κἂν γοῦν εἰς τὰ μέτρια
   λυπεῖσθαι, βοηθουμένη. Ἡβηκὼς μὲν γὰρ ἤδη καὶ ὑπερτενὴς ὁ στάχυς,
   Θεριζέτω τις ἤδη μονονουχὶ καὶ ἐφθέγγετο, καὶ ὁ μὲν ἀρόσας τὴν γῆν,
   ἐφέστιον ἤδη τὸν ἀμητῆρα λαβὼν, ζωννυμένῳ πρὸς ἔργον ἐτέρπετο, τάχα δὲ
   καὶ οὐκ ἀρκέσειν αὐτῷ τὴν ἅλω 77.565 πολλάκις διελογίζετο. Τὰ δὲ ἦν ὄναρ,
   ἣ σκιὰ καὶ χαλάζης ἔργον, οὐ θεριστοῦ. Ὁ δὲ περιχεῖσθαι τοῖς ἀγαθοῖς ἤδη
   δοκῶν, πάντων εὐθὺς ἔρημος ἦν· ἀντὶ δὲ τῶν σταχύων χαλάζῃ πλουτῶν,
   πολύ τι καὶ μέγα τῆς ἐλπίδος ἐσφάλλετο. Κώμη δὲ ἡ ταύτης γείτων καὶ
   ὅμορος ἡμερωτέραν νοσήσασα τὴν ὀργὴν, τοὺς μὲν ἐπὶ τοῖς ἀρότροις
   ὀδύρεται πόνους, μακρὸν δὲ καὶ πλατὺ γεωργήσασα λήϊον, πλοῦτον ἡγεῖται
   πρὸς τὸ παρὸν τὴν εἰς κόρον τροφὴν, μᾶλλον δὲ τὴν πολύ τι καὶ λίαν
   ἀποδέουσαν κόρου. δʹ. Τίς οὖν ἡ τούτων κατασκεψώμεθα αἰτία, εἰδῶ μεν ἀπὸ
   τῆς θείας Γραφῆς. Οὐκοῦν ἐρεῖ πάλιν ἡμῖν ὁ πάντων ἔχων τὴν ἐξουσίαν· "Αἱ
   ὁδοί σου, καὶ τὰ ἐπιτηδεύματά σου ἐποίησαν ταῦτά σοι· αὕτη ἡ κακία σου, ὅτι
   πικρὰ, ὅτι ἥψατο ἕως τῆς καρδίας σου." Ἀκολουθεῖ γὰρ τοῖς πλημμελήμασιν
   ἐκτόπως, τὸ χρῆναι δικαίως κολάζεσθαι, καὶ ταῖς παρ' ἡμῖν ἀπο νοίαις
   ἰσοστατεῖν ἀνάγκη τὴν δίκην. Ἀποπαυσώμεθα τοίνυν παντὸς ἀνοσίου
   τολμήματος· "Συγκόψωμεν, καθὼς γέγραπται, τὰς ῥομφαίας εἰς ἄροτρα, καὶ
   τὰς ζιβύνας εἰς δρέπανα·" καὶ, ὥς φησιν ὁ Μελῳδὸς, "∆εῦτε, προσκυνήσωμεν,
   καὶ προσπέσωμεν αὐτῷ," καὶ δεδακρυμένοι λέγωμεν· "Ἡμάρτομεν, ἠνομίσα
   μεν, ἠδικήσαμεν." Τότε γὰρ, τότε καὶ ἵλεως ἔσται Θεός· καὶ ἀποστήσει μὲν
   τὴν ὀργὴν, εὑρήσει δὲ πάλιν ἡ γῆ, καὶ δώροις ἡμᾶς τοῖς κατὰ συνήθειαν

   εὐφρανεῖ. "Οὐ γὰρ ἔχομεν ἀρχιερέα, μὴ δυνάμενον συμπαθῆσαι ταῖς ἀνομίαις
   ἡμῶν," κατὰ τὴν τοῦ Παύλου φωνήν· "πεπειρασμένον δὲ καθ' ὁμοιότητα
   χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας." Ὅτι γὰρ ἔνεστι προχείρως ἐποι κτείρειν ἐθέλειν τῷ
   Μονογενεῖ, πόνου μὲν οἶμαι δεήσειν ἐμοὶ πρὸς τὸ δύνασθαι πείθειν οὐδενός·
   ἑτοι μότατα δὲ καὶ ὑμᾶς συγκατανεύειν ὑπολαμβάνειν, τῆς εἰς ἡμᾶς
   ἀγαπήσεως περιαθροῦντας τὸ μέτρον, καὶ ὧν δι' ἡμᾶς ὑπέμεινεν ἐννοῦντας
   τὸ μέγεθος. Ἐπειδὴ γὰρ ἦμεν ἅπαντες οἱ τόνδε τὸν περίγειον οἰκοῦντες
   χῶρον, ἀνανταγωνίστῳ πλεονεξίᾳ τῇ τοῦ τυραννήσαντος δαίμονος, ἰχθύων
   δίκην σεσαγηνευμέ νοι πρὸς ὄλεθρον καὶ ἀπώλειαν, γέγονεν ἄνθρωπος ὁ
   Μονογενὴς, ἵνα πάντας ἐξέληται, "καὶ κηρύξῃ μὲν αἰχμαλώτοις ἄφεσιν,
   τυφλοῖς δὲ ἀνάβλεψιν, ὡς αὐτός πού φησι, καλέσῃ δὲ πρὸς τοῦτο καὶ
   ἐνιαυτὸν Κυρίου δεκτόν." Οὐκοῦν ἐλεήμων ὁ Μονογενὴς, εἰ καὶ τῆς
   οἰκονομίας τὸν τρόπον οὐ συνιέντες οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι το σοῦτον ἀπέσχον τοῦ κἂν
   ὅλως ἐθελῆσαι τοῦτον λαβεῖν, ὡς ποτὲ μὲν ὑβρίζοντας καὶ Σαμαρείτην
   ἀποκαλεῖν, ποτὲ δὲ πάλιν ἀφορήτως λελυπηκότας, καὶ εἰς ξένην
   καταπηδῶντας μανίαν, καὶ καταλεύειν ἤδη τολμᾷν. Ἐπειδὴ δὲ θεομαχοῦντας
   ἐλέγχων, καὶ τῆς ἀκρίτου μανίας ἀνεπυνθάνετο παρ' αὐτῶν τὴν αἰτίαν ὁ
   Κύριος λέγων· "Πολλὰ καλὰ ἔδειξα ἔργα ὑμῖν παρὰ τοῦ 77.568 Πατρός μου·
   διὰ ποίων αὐτῶν ἔργων λιθάζετέ με;" παραληροῦντες ἔφασκον· "Περὶ καλοῦ
   ἔργου οὐ λι θάζομέν σε, ἀλλὰ περὶ βλασφημίας, ὅτι σὺ, ἄνθρωπος ὢν, ποιεῖς
   σεαυτὸν Θεόν." Εἶτα, τί πρὸς αὐτοὺς ὁ Σωτήρ; "Εἰ οὐ ποιῶ τὰ ἔργα τοῦ Πατρός
   μου, μὴ πιστεύετέ μοι, εἰ δὲ ποιῶ, κἂν ἐμοὶ μὴ πιστεύητε, τοῖς ἔργοις μου
   πιστεύετε." Οὐ γὰρ ἐξ ὧν ὡς ἄνθρω πος τοῖς ὁρῶσιν ἐφαίνετο, δοκιμάζεσθαι
   τὰ καθ' ἑαυτὸν ἠξίου, ἀλλ' ἐξ ὧν ὁ Θεὸς εἰργάζετο, οὐκ ἐπακτὸν ἔχων τὸ τῆς
   θεότητος ἀξίωμα, καθάπερ ἡμεῖς, ὅταν ἡμᾶς λέγῃ ἡ θεία Γραφὴ θεούς·
   οὐσιωδῶς δὲ μᾶλλον ἐνυπάρχων αὐτῷ, ἅ τε δὴ καὶ ὄντι κατὰ φύ σιν Θεῷ, καὶ
   τῆς τοῦ γεννήσαντος ἰδιότητος κληρο νόμῳ. Ἔχει δὲ καὶ τὸ πάντα δύνασθαι
   δρᾷν, οὐ παρ' ἑτέρου λαβὼν, ἀλλ' ὡς τῶν δυνάμεων Κύριος, καὶ ἐκ τῆς
   οὐσίας τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ Πατρός. Εἰ γὰρ καὶ γέγονεν ἄνθρωπος, διὰ τὴν ἀγάπην
   τὴν εἰς ἡμᾶς, ἀλλ' οὐκ ἀγνοήσωμεν διὰ τοῦτο τῶν ἁπάντων Κύριον, οὐδὲ τὸ
   κατὰ φύσιν εἶναι Θεὸν τὸν Ἐμμανουὴλ ἐκπέμψομεν, ἀλλ' οὐδὲ τοῖς
   Ἰουδαίοις τὰ ἴσα φρονοῦντες ἐγκαλέσομεν αὐτῷ τὴν δι' ἡμᾶς ἀνθρω πότητα·
   οὐδὲ ἐροῦμεν, ἀνοσίως ἀπαιτιώμενοι τὸν δι' ἡμᾶς γεγονότα καθ' ἡμᾶς χωρὶς
   ἁμαρτίας· Οὐκ ἄν σε προσκυνήσομεν, ἐπείπερ, ἄνθρωπος ὢν, ποιεῖς σεαυ τὸν
   Θεόν. Ἦν γὰρ, καὶ ἔστι, καὶ ἔσται Θεὸς κατὰ φύσιν, καὶ πρὸ σαρκὸς καὶ μετὰ
   σαρκός. Ἐπιμαρτυ ρήσει δὲ καὶ ὁ Παῦλος γράφων· "Χριστὸς χθὲς καὶ σήμερον,
   ὁ αὐτὸς καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας." Ὁρᾷς πῶς οὐκ εἰς Υἱῶν δυάδα κατατεμὼν
   εὑρίσκεται τὸν Ἐμμανουὴλ, οὐδὲ γυμνῷ καθ' ἑαυτὸν ὄντι τυχὸν, τῷ ἐκ Θεοῦ
   καὶ Πατρὸς ἀπαστράψαντι Λόγῳ, τὸ ὡσαύτως ἔχειν διαπαντὸς ἀπονέμει· ἀλλ'
   Υἱὸν ἔνα καὶ μόνον κατὰ φύσιν
